blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: With an overhead system, basement drains no longer connect to the sewer by gravity. The floor drain and basement fixtures empty into a sealed pit. An [ejector pump](/geneva/ejector-pump) lifts the water to a pipe near the ceiling, a check valve stops it from falling back and it leaves the house above the level the sewer can reach.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewers and Geneva's Older Basements
blocks.intro: Geneva's older homes are the most likely to need one.

items.h3: Deep Basements Below the Street Sewer
items.body: Many 19th-century homes near the Fox River have basements that sit well below the sewer in the street. Any surcharge finds the floor drain.
Old fieldstone and brick foundations need careful planning for the pit and the pipe path. We assess the basement before we quote.
About 9 inches of rain fell on Geneva in two days. A storm like that overwhelms gravity drains.
We camera your line before recommending a conversion. If a root mass or break is the cause, a [sewer repair](/geneva/sewer-repair) may be all you need.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer Questions From Geneva Homeowners

items.q: Can an overhead sewer go in a historic basement?
items.answer: Usually. Older basements can have stone walls and tight layouts, so we plan the pit and pipe path before quoting.

items.q: Does an overhead sewer stop groundwater?
items.preview: No. That's a sump pump's job.
items.answer: No. It stops sewer backups. Groundwater needs a [sump pump](/geneva/sump-pumps).
Yes. It drains to the new pit with the rest of the basement.
Usually a few days, depending on layout and finishes.
